articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Related to North Korea and DRC
body: On October 28, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The North Korea designations specifically targeted ten individuals and one entity for allegedly supporting government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes that defraud U.S. companies and generate revenue for North Korea's weapons and missile programs.

Four individuals were designated pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13687, while the entity and six individuals were designated under E.O. 13722. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks funding Pyongyang's proliferation activities and address human rights abuses in the DRC.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations stemmed from exports to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer between September 2018 and March 2022. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed but egregious, leading to a civil penalty.
The settlement amount for Extreme Networks, Inc. was $1,529,685, highlighting the continued enforcement of sanctions against companies dealing with designated Russian entities.

The amendments likely address common questions and scenarios encountered by those subject to OFAC regulations, offering updated interpretations or clarifications on existing policies.
These FAQs are a crucial resource for compliance professionals, helping them navigate the complexities of sanctions enforcement and reporting requirements to avoid potential violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran, Russia GLs; Designates Iran; Removes Belarus, North Korea Designations
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of significant actions, including new Iran-related designations, the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, and the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations.

The Iran-related designations target specific individuals or entities, further restricting their access to the U.S. financial system. Concurrently, the new General Licenses for Iran and Russia aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, potentially to facilitate humanitarian aid or other specific activities.

The removal of designations for certain entities or individuals related to Belarus and North Korea indicates a recalibration of sanctions policy, which could be a response to changed circumstances or diplomatic engagements.

articles.headline: PAIPA Designations Issued with Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.
PAIPA targets individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property, aiming to safeguard U.S. economic interests and technological advantage.

The accompanying General Licenses are intended to mitigate unintended consequences of the designations, allowing for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, ensuring that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has paid an $11,662,930 civil penalty to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for 475 apparent sanctions violations.

These violations, occurring between September 2021 and April 2025, involved approximately $14.83 million in transactions across various sanctions programs, including those related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations included payments through blocked banks, flaws in alert prioritization, delays in watchlist updates, and mishandling of accounts. OFAC classified the case as non-egregious but applied no reduction for remedial measures or cooperation, citing recklessness and harm to U.S. foreign policy as aggravating factors.

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Pause Rate Hikes in October Amid Persistent Inflation Concerns
body: Most global central banks largely maintained their interest rates in October, following a series of aggressive hikes in September. This pause comes as policymakers continue to grapple with persistent inflationary pressures, particularly driven by rising energy prices.

Canada's central bank was the only one among the G10 economies to raise rates in October, while the U.S. Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of Japan all held steady. The October lull followed a busy September, which saw six G10 central banks deliver a combined 150 basis points of hikes.

Despite the pause, analysts and policymakers signal that the tightening cycle may not be over, with ongoing concerns about inflation remaining above central bank targets. The Riksbank in Sweden, however, raised its policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2 percent on November 4, citing stronger economic activity and cost increases due to supply disruptions.

articles.headline: Fed Chair Warsh Warns Inflation Remains Too High Amid Rising Energy Prices
body: U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh issued a warning on October 28, 2026, stating that inflation remains unacceptably high, having consistently exceeded the central bank's 2% target for nearly six years.

Speaking after the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted to maintain the benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4%, Warsh emphasized the committee's focus on curbing price pressures. He noted that energy and related prices have continued to climb in recent weeks, posing a risk of broader economic inflation.

Despite strong economic growth, with third-quarter GDP appearing to accelerate, Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to ensuring that relative price changes in specific sectors do not spread across the entire economy and that inflation expectations remain anchored.

articles.headline: Russian Strikes Disrupt Water and Power in Kyiv; Death Toll Rises in Southern Ukraine
body: Overnight Russian attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine have caused hours-long power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions on Wednesday. This comes as rescuers continue to search for survivors in southern Ukraine, three days after one of the deadliest attacks in nearly five years of war.

On Monday, multiple Russian guided bombs struck a school and shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, resulting in 37 confirmed deaths and an estimated 38 people still trapped. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated the death toll in Komyshuvakha had risen to 40, with 30 more potentially buried in the rubble.

Kyiv's water utility company reported that city water supplies had been restored, and emergency centers were established to provide hot tea and charging points. Ukraine's air force reported downing or suppressing 272 out of 310 Russian drones, including 81 jet-powered drones, used in the overnight attacks.

articles.headline: China Intensifies Diplomatic Efforts in Middle East Amid US-Iran Tensions
body: China has intensified its diplomatic engagement across the Middle East as the prospect of renewed U.S. attacks on Iran raises concerns among Gulf governments. Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq in Beijing, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi held separate talks with senior Iranian and Saudi officials.

Beijing also announced plans to dispatch three senior envoys to seven countries across the Middle East, underscoring its substantial economic interests in the region, including energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, regional investments, and export markets.

These diplomatic efforts coincide with preparations for a meeting between President Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump later this month, highlighting China's desire for a greater role in shaping regional security arrangements.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

This penalty, the largest in OCC history, stems from the bank's failure to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to the late filing of numerous suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with systemic breakdowns in internal controls, despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address these issues.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC determined that the bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to ensure compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations. Deficiencies included inadequate resources, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient training.

These failures contributed to the bank's processing of approximately $13 billion in suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade, including suspicious card charges and associated repayments.

articles.headline: DHS Adds BGI Genomics and Related Entities to UFLPA Entity List
body: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), on behalf of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), announced the addition of three related Chinese genomics companies to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List, effective October 29, 2026.

The newly listed entities are BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Genomics), MGI Tech Co., Ltd. (also known as MGI), and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Group and BGI Holdings). These companies were added under sections 2(d)(2)(B)(ii) and 2(d)(2)(B)(v) of the UFLPA.

This designation means that goods produced by these entities are subject to a rebuttable presumption of being prohibited from entering the United States due to their activities, which include sourcing materials from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region or working with the Xinjiang government to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
